analysis.one_liner: Cuts four major power plant pollutants, including mercury and carbon dioxide, by 2007.
analysis.headline: The bill had 134 cosponsors from both parties, but it never received a hearing or a vote and died in a House subcommittee at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Smokestacks Act would have required every power plant 15 megawatts or larger that burns fuel to cut sulfur dioxide by 75%, nitrogen oxide by 75%, mercury by 90%, and carbon dioxide back down to 1990 levels by January 2007. It also closed a loophole that let decades-old plants run without modern pollution controls, forcing any plant older than 30 years to meet current standards. It died after being referred to a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe air downwind of coal-fired power plants: children, older adults, and people with asthma or heart disease. Pollution from these plants causes smog, acid rain, fine soot, mercury contamination in fish, and climate emissions, and the bill would have sharply reduced all four. Electricity consumers in the long run could also benefit as plants switched to cleaner and more efficient sources.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living downwind of coal plants

how_it_helps.text: Requires aggregate sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants to fall 75% and nitrogen oxide to fall 75% by January 2007, cutting the pollution that causes acid rain, smog, and fine-particle soot.

Requires a 90% cut in mercury emissions from power plants, the largest uncontrolled industrial source of mercury, which contaminates fish and is especially dangerous to pregnant women and young children.
Requires power plant carbon dioxide emissions to return to 1990 levels by 2007, a mandatory cap on the greenhouse gas from the electric sector.
Requires any plant that has been operating for 30 years to meet modern new source performance standards, closing the grandfathering loophole that let old, dirty plants keep running for decades.
Directs EPA to include incentives for renewable energy in the regulations and to coordinate on energy efficiency to lower the cost of compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-burning power plants would bear the cost of installing scrubbers, mercury controls, and other equipment, or retiring their oldest units, and much of that cost would be passed to electricity customers. Coal mining communities would face reduced demand for coal.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal plant owners, then electricity customers

drawbacks.text: Compliance would cost power plant owners billions of dollars and some of it would show up on household electricity bills, especially in coal-dependent regions of the Midwest and South.

The compliance deadline of 2007 was ambitious; utilities and some regulators argued such large, simultaneous reductions could strain reliability and require rushed retirements of plants that supply power.
The bill's targets were fixed in law before EPA studies were complete, leaving regulators little flexibility to adjust the goals if costs or technical realities turned out worse than expected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case was strong: coal plants were a leading source of mercury, acid rain, and soot, and old plants had been exempt from modern standards since 1970, so the bill mainly targeted units that had avoided controls for 30 years. The real costs, higher electricity prices and job losses in coal communities, were genuine and fell hardest on coal-dependent regions, though the bill gave EPA flexibility in how reductions were allocated and relied partly on trading and efficiency to lower costs. On balance this was a public-health bill whose costs were real but localized, and whose benefits were broad but invisible to most voters.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its energy subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Clean Smokestacks Act on March 27, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It picked up 134 cosponsors, including 117 of 208 House Democrats, 16 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent.
On April 16, 2001, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and no further action of any kind was taken on it for the rest of the 107th Congress.
The bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without ever coming to a vote in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of aging coal-fired power plants and the coal industry came out ahead, since no emission cuts or modernization requirements were ever enacted, and the plants kept operating under the old standards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal plant owners and the coal industry

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 16 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Boehlert, Shays, Gilchrest, Saxton, and Roukema.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and allowed it to go only to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: In March 2001 he withdrew a campaign pledge to regulate power plant carbon dioxide, signaling administration opposition to mandatory CO2 caps while the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily but not entirely partisan: 117 of 208 House Democrats signed on versus 16 of 223 House Republicans, and the House never voted, so no roll-call shows how the rest would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would have required 75% cuts in sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, a 90% cut in mercury, and a carbon dioxide cap, plus modernization of any plant over 30 years old, all at major expense to utilities that relied on old coal units. Its defeat preserved their existing cost structure, with the pollution burden falling on the public.
Deep cuts in coal plant emissions would have reduced demand for coal; the bill's failure kept coal demand and production on the pre-existing path.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and emissions-control equipment makers
industries.note: The bill required renewable-energy incentives in EPA's regulations and would have driven purchases of scrubbers and mercury controls; these industries gained nothing because the bill never advanced.
